10221-purple-springs:
Nellie L. McClung published this Canadian novel in 1921, setting much of it on the prairie in a hard winter. Pearl Watson faces a long-awaited choice on the first of March, while her family waits out cold, debt, and tangled hopes. The title points to a place and a season of change, as spring breaks the grip of frost.

Chapters follow doctors, neighbors, lost love, and a woman known as the woman of Purple Springs. Old wrongs surface, plans collapse, and new paths open through work, care, and plain courage. Readers get a warm, moral tale of prairie women, family duty, and second chances.
10493-the-old-bush-songs:
A. B. Paterson, author of The Man from Snowy River, edited this collection of old bush songs in 1906, in a second impression completing ten thousand copies. The songs were composed and sung in bushranging, digging, and overlanding days, and Paterson gathered them before they faded. The book preserves a rough, musical Australia.

Two Aboriginal songs, Paddy Malone, the old bullock dray, the wild colonial boy, Bold Jack Donahoo, and the road to Gundagai stand among the pieces. Squatters, selectors, and sheep-washers sing their lives. Readers get a lively, historic songbook of the Australian bush.
10817-anne-severn-and-the-fieldings:
May Sinclair published Anne Severn and the Fieldings in 1922, a novel of an English family across the years. Anne Severn comes again to the Fieldings after her mother's death, asking at once for Jerrold, who peeks in and slips away, afraid to face her grief. Chapters follow Anne with Jerrold, Robert, Eliot, Colin, Queenie, Adeline, and Maisie.

Sinclair traces love, loyalty, and misunderstanding among the Fieldings from childhood to adult life. Her style is clear and psychological, attentive to inner feeling. Readers get a thoughtful family novel from a leading modernist of the 1920s.
10931-the-lullaby-with-original-engravin:
Short songs and verses for bedtime fill this small illustrated book from New London publisher John R. Bolles. An evening song opens the collection, with twilight dew on roses, birds in the nest, and a child guarded through the night. Robins, a yellow bird, a speckled hen with ten chickens, and a hurt lamb follow in simple rhymed stanzas.

Engravings face the verses, giving mothers and children pictures to look at while singing. The tone is gentle and devout, with prayers for protection and praise for small creatures. As an early American children's book, it shows what families read aloud at bedtime: short, musical lines, familiar animals, and a calm close to the day.
1139-fisherman-s-luck-and-some-other-unc:
Henry van Dyke loved rod and stream, and he gathers essays on fishing and on the luck that comes with it. His subjects are trout streams, camp talk, and the small mishaps of a day outdoors. The title essay argues that the best luck is the kind a patient angler makes for himself.

Other pieces touch on books, nature, and the art of taking holidays well. Van Dyke writes with a minister's warmth and a sportsman's eye, and his prose is gentle and unhurried. The book suits readers who fish, or who simply like to dream of quiet waters.
1210-kwaidan-stories-and-studies-of-stra:
Lafcadio Hearn, a Greek-born writer who made Japan his home, gathers ghost stories and studies of the strange: snow women, faceless ghosts, and spirits who keep old vows. The tales come from Japanese folklore, retold in Hearn's musical English with notes on their sources.

Hearn treats the supernatural as part of daily life, not as a trick, and his stories are quiet, eerie, and sad rather than shocking. The book introduced many Western readers to Japanese ghosts. It remains the classic English doorway into Japan's uncanny lore. Hearn's quiet, eerie tales still open the door to Japan's ghost lore.
12197-mr-scraggs:
Henry Wallace Phillips, author of Red Saunders, published Mr. Scraggs in 1906, introducing his hero through Red Saunders himself. The Grafton Press issued the book after magazine publication in 1903 to 1905.

Chapters follow Mr. Scraggs by proxy, in the toils, as St. Nicholas Scraggs, at the siege of the drug store, and at the fountain of youth. Scraggs, a small-town schemer with a big heart, talks his way into and out of trouble, with Red Saunders watching and commenting. Phillips writes in the same tall-talk manner as his western stories, mixing farce with sentiment. The book is a minor comic novel, best enjoyed as a companion to Red Saunders.
12791-wells-brothers-the-young-cattle-ki:
Andy Adams wrote Wells Brothers in 1911 about two orphaned brothers who claim a range and build a cattle business from the bottom rung. The story opens in 1885, when a trail herd leaves Dodge City for the Northwest and an accident strands the boys on the Beaver. A hospital camp, winter drifts, and an Indian scare test them.

Work scenes give the book its flavour: salting beef into barrels, roping steers, holding the fort through winter, and harvesting on the range. The brothers rise by steady labour rather than luck. Adams, himself a former drover, writes with rare authority on trail life.
13031-indian-games-and-dances-with-nativ:
Alice C. Fletcher, of Harvard's Peabody Museum, arranged this 1915 book from Native American ceremonials and sports for young readers. It is dedicated to the youth of America. Part one gives dances and songs, led by the Life of the Corn, a drama in five dances from speaking corn to honor for Mother Corn. Part two gives games of hazard, guessing, and ball.

Fletcher prints words, steps, and music, so groups can perform the dances as described. Singers sway in rhythm, leaders step forward in line, and a hidden-disk game turns on a player who works magic over the pieces. The book preserves Native song and play with care, while framing them for school and camp use in its own time.
13167-more-cricket-songs:
Norman Gale's 1905 volume of cricket songs follows his earlier Cricket Songs, and he dedicates it to John Denton, a boy he once scolded for pouting through arithmetic. Gale, once a schoolmaster, promises that the only sums here are those of the telegraph, meaning scores. Thanks go to editors and to Prince Ranjitsinhji for leave to reprint.

Songs toast the lad with a useful fifteen, the thrifty bowler, and the bat who rules the green with a thundering fifty. Other verses look back to Arthur's court, where knights hammered helms for love and glory, and to birds that sing over the nets. Gale's verse is light, musical, and fond of the game, written for players and watchers alike.
13341-hymns-and-spiritual-songs:
Isaac Watts's Hymns and Spiritual Songs, in three books, gathers hymns collected from Scripture, composed on divine subjects, and prepared for the Lord's Supper. This text follows an 1818 London printing, keeping the index and the table of Scriptures turned into verse. Watts, the great English hymn writer, gives congregations songs for worship and private devotion.

One hymn has Wisdom say, happy the man who keeps her ways, while the man who shuns them dies. Another calls all harmonious tongues to sing Christ, everlasting God and man, who took flesh to take away guilt, while waves of grief rolled over his bosom. The collection shaped English Protestant singing for generations, and many of its hymns are still sung.
13439-divine-songs:
Isaac Watts writes songs for children in easy language, hoping young voices will learn praise, duty, and faith by singing. Dedicated to the daughters of Sir Thomas Abney, who gave Watts shelter for his health, the book sets short verses on prayer, thanks, and the gospel.

Children sing of being born into Christian teaching rather than heathen worship. Of kings and prophets who longed to hear what Christ revealed, and of knowledge, virtue, truth, and grace as robes that never fade. Watts keeps words simple and lines short, so that a child can grasp the sense while learning to sing. The songs shaped English Sunday school verse for generations.
13647-nonsense-songs:
Edward Lear filled this book with rhymed nonsense songs, short stories, botany jokes, and alphabets. It grew from his earlier nonsense books for children and adults alike. Animals talk, travel, marry, and misbehave in neat, musical verses. Made-up plants and odd alphabets sit beside the songs, each with its own small drawing in the print edition.

Favourites include the Owl and the Pussy-Cat, the Duck and the Kangaroo, and the Jumblies. Other pieces send four small children around the world and invent creatures that never existed. Lear keeps the rhymes simple and the images bold. The humour comes from calm logic applied to absurd events. It still works well read aloud, line by line.
138-george-sand-some-aspects-of-her-life:
René Doumic sketches the French novelist George Sand in ten chapters, from Aurore Dupin to the good lady of Nohant. Translated by Alys Hallard and first published in 1910, the book disclaims any full biography. It offers aspects instead: feminist, romantic, humanitarian, and writer.

Chapters follow Sand's break with convention, her friendships, her 1848 hopes, and her late calm at Nohant. Doumic weighs her genius and her influence without worship or scorn. Illustrations from portraits and engravings accompany the text. The volume suits readers meeting Sand for the first time. Doumic's sketches invite readers to try Sand's novels next.
13820-unhappy-far-off-things:
Lord Dunsany published Unhappy Far-Off Things in 1919, a book of war sketches and poems. A sonnet, A Dirge of Victory, opens it, bidding victory blow its trumpet not over battalions but over hollows full of old wire. Long-dead soldiers wait among weeds, mud, and shattered iron. Winter cracked bones no man heeds.

Prose pieces follow a traveller through trenches guarded only by fungi, past nettles and small unnatural valleys. Clicking iron breaks the silence of the waste. Dunsany writes with fantasy's eye turned to real ruin. The book mourns the dead rather than celebrating triumph. It stands as a quiet, powerful war memorial in prose and verse.
1416-mrs-lirriper-s-lodgings:
Mrs Lirriper returns in this companion volume, telling how she carried on her lodging-house business after her husband's death. In her own voice she describes lodgers good and bad, rents in arrears, and the daily work of keeping a respectable house in London, all with humour and a warm heart.

Her lodgers' stories, including that of a young man she takes under her wing, fill the book with incident and feeling. Mrs Lirriper's plain sense and kindness hold the whole together. It is a gentle, funny portrait of a working woman and the small world she rules from her parlour.
14869-soldier-songs-and-love-songs:
A. H. Laidlaw's 1898 volume, dedicated to the soldiers and sailors of the United States, mixes soldier songs with love songs in short, singable pieces. Custer, the American girl, the good ship Ohio and the Union oath open a sequence of patriotic and romantic lyrics.

Betsie Brown, the sword of Jehovah, black eyes and the American Ca Ira follow. A bird of the summering north, the war song of William the Conqueror and the light of beautiful eyes come next. The flag of brothers, a dying soldier to the nightingale and Burke of the brave brigade keep the martial thread. Laidlaw writes plainly for voice and memory, and the book reads as a period songbook of flag and feeling.
15211-some-broken-twigs:
Clara Beede's 1946 poetry book, printed at Cleveland, is dedicated to her granddaughter Betty Todd Bristow, the new mother. A sonnet to New York opens the set, praising youth who struggle on ambition's tour and recalling pioneers who tamed wilderness with ax and spade. Broken twigs mark trails others fought.

Beede's verse links past builders to present hope, urging readers to retrace paths and plan future life with courage. Her lines are plain, rhymed, and earnest, with a homely, patriotic warmth. Fans of mid-century occasional verse will find the book modest, heartfelt, and easy to read.
15370-bab-ballads-and-savoy-songs:
W. S. Gilbert gathered his comic verse and opera songs in this volume, published in Philadelphia. The Bab Ballads are short, absurd tales in rhyme, while the Savoy songs come from his operas with Arthur Sullivan. Both halves share Gilbert's neat meter and his taste for turning rank, law, and polite life upside down.

Familiar pieces include the yarn of the Nancy Bell, the tale of Captain Reece, and songs such as the Modern Major-General, the Policeman's Lot, and the Lord Chancellor's Song. Bishops, sailors, policemen, and lords all meet comic ruin or comic triumph. The book works as a single showcase for Gilbert's humor: clever rhyme, mock logic, and a sharp eye for English institutions, best read aloud.
15389-true-riches-or-wealth-without-wing:
T. S. Arthur's 1852 book True Riches, or Wealth Without Wings, first bore the title Riches Without Wings, until Arthur learned a similar volume was about to appear in a new edition. He changed the title rather than clash with it. The book, printed at Boston, teaches that true wealth lies in character, home, and faith, not in money that flies away.

Arthur writes in the moral domestic style that made him popular, with tales of families tempted by riches and saved by virtue. His lessons are plain, earnest, and very much of the 1850s. Readers of early American moral fiction will find the book sincere, homely, and full of period feeling.
157-daddy-long-legs:
Jerusha Abbott, the oldest orphan at the John Grier Home, wins a secret patron for college. Jean Webster's Daddy-Long-Legs, copyrighted in 1912, tells her story through letters to the trustee she knows only by his long shadow. She must write, study, and grow without ever meeting him.

At college Jerusha renames herself Judy, makes friends, reads widely, and falls for a young man named Jervis. Her letters mix humor, ambition, and sharp views on charity and work. The final letters reveal who her patron truly is. The epistolary novel charmed readers and inspired stage and film versions.
15766-the-claverings:
A novel by Anthony Trollope, first serialised in the Cornhill Magazine from February 1866 to May 1867, then issued in book form by Smith, Elder and Company. Trollope, a master of social fiction, sets his tale among clergy, gentry, and county families. Harry Clavering must choose a profession and, harder still, a wife. The novel runs to forty-eight chapters of careful social comedy.

Harry wavers between Florence Burton, steady and true, and Julia Brabazon, now Lady Ongar, rich, widowed, and dazzling. A rector, a captain, a count, and a supposed Russian spy stir the plot around them. Trollope weighs prudence against passion, and duty against charm, with his usual calm irony. The book rewards readers who like character drawn slowly, through talk, letters, and small decisions.
1595-whirligigs:
O. Henry's Whirligigs gathers stories from the world and the door to a technical error. It includes the famous Ransom of Red Chief, in which two kidnappers find their young captive far worse than any ransom. Calloway's Code, A Matter of Mean Elevation, and Girl show O. Henry in Western, city, and comic moods.

The title points to the book's spinning surprises: plots that turn on a letter, a code, or a sudden reversal. The stories are brisk and humane. Whirligigs is a strong O. Henry collection, and the Red Chief tale alone has made it a lasting favourite.
17009-studies-in-occultism-a-series-of-r:
H. P. Blavatsky's studies in occultism, number one in a series of reprints from her writings, issued by the Aryan Theosophical Press at Point Loma, California, in 1910. Contents hold Practical Occultism from Lucifer, April 1888, Occultism versus the Occult Arts from May 1888, and The Blessings of Publicity from August 1891. A motto says occultism is not magic, though magic is one of its tools, nor the pursuit of happiness, for its first step is sacrifice.

Blavatsky defines occultism as the science of life, the art of living, served by psychic and mental powers but not ruled by them. Her essays mix theosophy, ethics, and warning against mere wonder-seeking. Readers keen on theosophy will find a short, primary source, best read as a statement of Blavatsky's own teaching, not as settled science.
17585-english-embroidered-bookbindings:
Cyril Davenport, author of The English Regalia, wrote this study of English embroidered bookbindings, edited by Alfred Pollard and published in London in 1899 by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner and Company. Pollard supplies a general introduction, and the book appears in The English Bookman's Library series. A contents and list of plates section guides readers through the examples.

Readers learn how embroidered covers were designed, stitched, and valued, with plates showing fine bindings of past centuries. Davenport writes as a keeper of such treasures, with a craftsman's eye for thread, design, and condition. The book suits book lovers, binders, and collectors who care about the outside of a book as much as its pages.
17773-slavery-s-passed-away-and-other-so:
Edward Harrigan's words and Dave Braham's music fill this song collection, headed by Slavery's Passed Away, as sung in Harrigan's drama Pete. Copyright in 1887 belonged to William A. Pond and Company. The file carries only the lyrics to the songs; music images, midi files, and Lilypond sources live in the fuller edition.

Readers get popular stage songs of the 1880s, including a title song that greets emancipation in the theatre's cheerful voice. The collection suits readers of Harrigan, of minstrel and vaudeville song, and of post-war popular music. Its lyrics preserve a stage world now largely vanished.
18173-tales-of-the-ridings:
F. W. Moorman wrote Tales of the Ridings, printed in London in 1921 by Elkin Mathews, with a memoir by Professor C. Vaughan. Moorman, late professor of English at Leeds, died in 1919, and this book gathers his Yorkshire tales as a memorial.

Stories include A Laocoon of the Rocks, Throp's Wife, The Inner Voice, and Corn-Fever, with a memoir tracing Moorman from Devon roots to Dartmoor childhood. Vaughan praises his love of birds, flowers, and country walks. The book is a warm, regional set of tales, best for readers who love Yorkshire speech, moors, and folk.
18260-more-tales-of-the-ridings:
F. W. Moorman, late professor of English at Leeds University and editor of Yorkshire Dialect Poems, published this 1920 set of tales of the Ridings, the old divisions of Yorkshire. Moorman writes in and about Yorkshire speech and custom, and his tales keep the voice of the dales. The volume appeared in London from Elkin Mathews.

Contents give Melsh Dick, two letters, a miracle, tales of a grandmother, the tree of knowledge, Janet's cove, the potato and the pig, and coals of fire. Melsh Dick, last survivor of the woodland divinities, guards unripe nuts in the Pennine woods, and parents once warned children that Melsh Dick would catch them at nutting. Readers get Yorkshire folklore in story form: fauns, grandmothers, and the greenwood fading before modern life.
18273-the-wild-tribes-of-davao-district-:
Fay-Cooper Cole wrote this 1913 Field Museum study of the peoples of the Davao District on Mindanao in the Philippines. Cole served as assistant curator of Malayan ethnology, and the work came out of the R. F. Cummings Philippine Expedition. A tribal map opens the volume, and photographs show tools, ornaments, and dress.

The study takes six groups in turn: the Bagobo, Bila-an, Kulaman, Tagakaolo, Ata, and Mandaya, then ends with a conclusion. Shell bracelets, brass anklets, ear plugs, rice mortars, and bamboo plate racks appear among the plates. A reader gets a detailed early survey of how these groups lived, worked, and marked their rank and kin.
18328-the-story-of-sigurd-the-volsung-an:
William Morris retold the Norse legend of Sigurd in this long poem, published by Longmans, Green in 1904 in an eighth impression. Morris takes the Volsung story from the old sagas and gives it in English verse, book by book. The poem stands as one of the great Victorian retellings of northern myth.

Book one follows Sigmund: the dwelling of King Volsung, the wedding of Signy, the fall of Volsung, the slaying of Siggeir the Goth-king, and the last battle of Sigmund. Book two, Regin, gives the birth of Sigurd, son of Sigmund, his horse Greyfell, and Regin's tale of kindred and accursed gold. Readers get the dragon, the treasure, and the fall of the Niblungs in Morris's rich, archaic verse.
18599-bully-and-bawly-no-tail-the-jumpin:
Howard R. Garis wrote this bedtime book in 1915, with pictures by Louis Wisa. It holds thirty-one short stories, one for each day of the month, about Bully and Bawly No-Tail, two jumping frogs. The tales first ran in the Newark Evening News, where children and parents praised them, before book publication.

Stories cover swimming, a water wheel, a big jump, Grandpa Croaker digging a well, marbles, a soldier hat, hunting, a church steeple, and a circus visit. Uncle Wiggily and other Garis favorites drop in along the way. The book suits reading aloud at bedtime, with short, funny adventures each night.
19948-potash-and-perlmutter-settle-thing:
Montague Glass created Abe Potash and Morris Perlmutter, New York garment partners. Settle Things, dated 1919, is a later volume of their comic doings. Morris blames a liberty roast at Wasserbauer's for Abe's indigestion. It was Königsburger Klops before the war renamed it, he notes. The renamed meatball gets Glass's whole method in one joke. Dialect, business, and friendship grind along together.

Potash and Perlmutter began as magazine stories and conquered Broadway. Their garment-trade quarrels are love in disguise. Glass wrote the New York clothing business from inside knowledge. The 1919 volume adds wartime flavor to the partnership. These stories remain classics of American ethnic humor. Their warmth has outlasted their dialect fashions.
2004-pigs-is-pigs:
Ellis Parker Butler builds a short comic tale on one stubborn fact of railway rules: two guinea pigs sent by express must be charged as pigs, whatever their size. Agent Mike Flannery will not bend the book, and sender Mr. Morehouse will not pay. Butler, an American humorist, built the tale on a real railway dispute over rates for small animals.

While the two men argue, the guinea pigs breed, and the bill grows with every litter. Butler keeps the joke running to its logical end, and the story stands as a neat satire on red tape and on men who would rather be right than sensible. The joke works because both men are right by their own rules, and neither will yield an inch to common sense.
20213-peace-on-earth-good-will-to-dogs:
Peace on Earth, Good-Will to Dogs is a Christmas tale with a twist in its title. It opens at twilight on Christmas Eve, a classic story hour. The writer jokes about that most conventional of all such openings. Yet he asks readers not to take the tale as mere cheek.

Dogs, as the title promises, share in the goodwill of the season. Christmas tales often widen their mercy to beasts as well as men. Kindness to a dog can crack a hard heart in such tales. Readers get holiday warmth with a soft spot for four-legged friends.
20352-the-jest-book-the-choicest-anecdot:
The Jest Book gathers the choicest anecdotes and sayings from old humor. It traces hearty laughter back to when Hamlet was king in Denmark. Jesters like Wamba, Will Somers, and Killigrew carried such jokes down. Joseph Miller then retold many over his pipe and tankard in Clare Market.

His delighted hearers at the Black Jack tavern loved those retellings nightly. Mark Lemon edited this Victorian store of wit for Punch readers. Short jokes, puns, and sharp replies fill its pages in ranks. Readers get centuries of English humor in one handy, laughing volume.
20777-r-caldecott-s-first-collection-of-:
John Gilpin's wild ride leads R. Caldecott's First Collection of Pictures and Songs. Mrs. Gilpin praises thrift, for wine is dear, and their own stock is bright and clear. Gilpin kisses his wife, glad she loves fun yet keeps a frugal mind.

Randolph Caldecott reshaped the picture book with swift, witty drawings. Rhymes, songs, and tales here pair short verse with lively art. Children of the 1880s met a new kind of book in his pages. The Caldecott Medal for picture books now bears his name, and this set shows why his work still sets the bar.
21426-the-tale-of-daddy-longlegs:
Daddy Longlegs puzzles his neighbours in Arthur Scott Bailey's Tale of Daddy Longlegs, a 1918 Tuck-Me-In Tale. Strange tracks start the tale, and the field and forest folk seek a wise answer. Old Mr Crow is away past Blue Mountain, so the mystery waits.

Bailey's short chapters suit reading aloud at bedtime. Daddy meets Mr Crow's scorn, a contest, and the rush of the ant soldiers. Harry L. Smith's drawings show the small cast at work and play. Like Bailey's other tales of Pleasant Valley, the book turns tiny creatures into clear, lively characters for young readers.
21773-four-meetings:
Four meetings, spread over years, are all the narrator gets of Caroline Spencer in this Henry James tale of 1885. He remembers each one clearly, for she made a deep impression on him. The first comes at a snowy Christmas tea party in the depths of New England. There he shows her photographs from Europe, brought home in great portfolios.

Caroline is quiet, bright, and pretty, a charming specimen of her type, the narrator says. Across the four meetings, James builds her whole fate from glances and brief talks. News of her death opens the tale and hangs over every scene. It is one of James's most tender short works, a life seen only in flashes, and loved all the more for that.
22364-the-philosophy-of-the-moral-feelin:
The Philosophy of the Moral Feelings studies why humans judge right and wrong. Its author gives the science two practical aims. One aim is the mental and moral culture of every rational being.

That aim, he says, bears directly on life at its highest stakes. The other aim links this science to revealed religion. Each, he argues, confirms and illustrates the other. Moral feeling thus becomes evidence for faith, and faith for morals. The book belongs to an age when philosophy and theology worked together. Readers get a period system for conscience, built to guide conduct and belief at once.
22804-apron-strings:
Eleanor Gates wrote Apron-Strings, a 1917 novel of family ties and the pull between a mother and the children grown beyond her strings. Gates, an American novelist and playwright, wrote warm, popular fiction about households under gentle strain, and weddings bring such strain to a head.

The sample opens with a florist's suspicion: I tell you, Steve, there's something funny about holding this wedding out on that scrap of lawn. The little man with the brown beard jerks his head toward the bay window. He sets down his basket of smilax on the drawing-room floor. Then he cuts the end off a cigar while he talks. Small talk, big secret: Gates builds her opening from the help's-eye view of a wedding. The novel that follows plays comedy and feeling in her practiced balance.
22838-country-lodgings:
A cottage view opens Country Lodgings, Mary Russell Mitford's sketch of village life. Between the foliage peeps a vine-covered cottage, while in the distance stands the Court, with its old porch, long windows, and tall clustered chimneys. The narrator calls it the prettiest prospect in all Aberleigh.

Into that pretty scene come lodgers, and with them the comedy of country hospitality. Rooms, rents, expectations, and village talk all get Mitford's close attention. She writes as a neighbor who knows every household and enjoys them all. The piece has little plot by design. Instead it offers a walk through a place and its people, guided by one of the sharpest, kindest observers in English village writing.
2306-uncle-remus-his-songs-and-his-sayin:
Joel Chandler Harris framed the tales of Brer Rabbit and his fellow creatures as told by Uncle Remus, a formerly enslaved storyteller, to a white child on a Georgia plantation. Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings preserves African American animal tales of trickery and survival, with Brer Rabbit outwitting the stronger Brer Fox and Brer Bear. The dialect, once praised for realism, now requires careful, critical reading.

The stories themselves, rooted in Black folklore, remain witty and subversive, with the weak winning by brains. Modern readers should approach the frame with an understanding of its plantation nostalgia. As folklore, the collection is a landmark of American storytelling.
23466-bartholomew-de-las-casas-his-life-:
Francis Augustus MacNutt wrote this nineteen hundred nine life of Bartholomew de Las Casas, the friar who fought for the native peoples of the Spanish Indies. A portrait by Enguidanos fronts the book, and a letter of fifteen fifty six to Carranza de Miranda shows Las Casas at his most defiant.

For forty years, he writes, he denounced the destruction of peoples to kings and councils a thousand times. No one yet proved him false or shamed him with a retraction. MacNutt traces his voyages, his preaching, his clashes with foes like Sepulveda, and his writings, with archives full of trials and reports as proof. Readers of colonial history will find a full, earnest portrait of a conscience that would not rest while an empire wronged its subjects.
23501-a-pair-of-clogs:
Amy Walton gathered these short stories under the title A Pair of Clogs. The set opens with a girl child stolen by gypsies, then given up and left in an outhouse owned by a young clergyman. His wife delights in the child, the pair raise her, and after some years, at a tense moment, her true mother is found.

An agreement follows, by which the child is shared between the two homes, and Walton draws a moral from the bargain without preaching. Other stories in the set keep the same warm, plain style, with country scenes and kind, flawed people. Young readers will enjoy the tales for their feeling and their twists, while grown readers will note Walton's gift for making a small domestic drama feel large and true.
23527-the-twelve-magic-changelings:
M. A. Glen made this nineteen hundred seven cut out book for children, printed in colours by Frederick A. Stokes of New York. Twelve magic changelings pair a figure with its mate. The pairs include Mary and her little lamb, Humpty Dumpty and the egg, Tom the Piper's son and his pig, and the town mouse and the country mouse.

Silverhair and the little wee bear, Robinson Crusoe and his parrot, the lion and the unicorn, and the witch and her black cat are among the pairs. Nancy Netticoat and the candle, Santa Claus and the Christmas tree, the frog who would a wooing go with the lily white duck, and Dick Whittington and his cat complete the set. Children cut out double figures, fold on dotted lines, and watch the pairs change. The book charms as a hands on toy, where scissor work turns old rhymes into moving pictures.
24744-the-valley-of-the-kings:
Marmaduke Pickthall wrote this novel, published at London in 1914 by J. M. Dent in the Wayfarers Library. Its frontispiece shows someone leaning above a man to inspect his work. The novel opens in the East, where the mother of Iskender holds her doorway in spitting defiance, cursing the mothers of nothing.

Across a sand-dell stands the white-walled Mission-house, above tamarisks, behind a hedge of prickly pear. Pickthall's tale follows East and West in collision, with faith, family, and empire at stake. Readers get a vivid, serious novel of the Levant, by a writer who knew it well.
24798-america-first-patriotic-readings:
Jasper L. McBrien, a Nebraska school chief turned federal school specialist, compiled this book of patriotic readings in 1916. It opens with a dramatization of the Continental Congress, then gathers speeches and poems for school use. Washington's Farewell Address and Lincoln's Second Inaugural stand beside Wilson on America first and the flag, plus pieces on Lee, the Blue and the Gray, and the reunited country.

Teachers could stage the Congress tableau or read single pieces at assemblies. The mix of history, verse, and oratory aimed to stir love of country in pupils of the World War era. The book now serves as a window into how American schools taught patriotism a century ago.
25215-three-things:
Elinor Glyn's Three Things, published in New York in 1915, is a book of essays on a changing social order. Glyn, a popular novelist, argues that unrest is a sign of life, not decay, and that civilized nations have made great gains against ignorance and disease in fifty years.

Later essays take up the responsibility of motherhood and the terms on which marriages stay happy. Glyn urges husbands and wives to keep the charms that first drew them together, rather than blame a partner for growing cold. The book speaks frankly, in its era's voice, about love, duty, and modern life.
25373-woodward-s-graperies-and-horticult:
Woodward's Graperies and Horticultural Buildings, by George E. Woodward and F. W. Woodward, architects and horticulturists, was published in New York in 1865. It offers designs and plain directions for glass houses in which grapes, flowers, and fruit can be forced or sheltered.

Contents cover position and forms of houses, heating by flues, steam, tanks, and hot-water pipes, hot beds, cold pits, and propagating houses. Twenty numbered designs follow, from small propagating houses to large ranges and orchard houses. The Woodwards report forty thousand cuttings rooted in one February with under one percent loss.
25453-how-the-fairy-violet-lost-and-won-:
Marianne L. B. Ker tells how a small fairy earns back her wings through kindness. Violet lives among violets at the foot of a stately oak, tending flowers with dew and a delicate brush. She paints petals, loosens heavy clay from roots, and dances with elves at night. Sister fairies Primrose and Cowslip share her forest home and play.

After her loss, Violet does a kindly deed each day, whispering lullabies to sleepers and soft words to wayfarers. In a crowded city she hears a sick child ask for a geranium in view, and Mother Nature watches her reward draw near. Griffith and Farran published the tale in 1872, illustrated by J. A. Martin.
26398-tudor-and-stuart-love-songs:
J. Potter Briscoe selected and edited this anthology of love lyrics from the Tudor and Stuart reigns. His introduction traces the songs to young Englishmen who travelled in France, Spain, and Italy during the Reformation years and brought home southern wit and verse. Sir Thomas Wyatt and the Earl of Surrey, courtiers of Henry VIII, gave England the Petrarchan sonnet, and amorous poetry took root in their wake.

The poems that follow sing of faithful and faithless lovers, partings, and returns, in the plain music of the period. Shepherds lament loves lost to a second and third rival, while other lyrics praise a mistress or bid farewell to untrue love. Briscoe's notes record small slips between contents list and text, such as Cherry Ripe and Julia swapping pages.
26500-anecdotes-of-dogs:
Edward Jesse's Anecdotes of Dogs, in an enlarged 1858 edition with engravings, celebrates the fidelity of dogs, which Pope held more richly storied than that of friends. Jesse, who gathered many original anecdotes, argues that the more the dog's character is known, the better his treatment will be and the stronger the sympathy for him. Friends contributed tales, notably Lady Morgan and Mrs. S. Carter Hall on the Irish wolf-dog.

Further anecdotes come from Colonel Hamilton Smith's Naturalist's Library, Captain Brown's sketches, and the Irish Penny Magazine's account of the wolf-dog. One tale shows dogs pointing a cat in comic earnest, while another notes a dog's unfortunate ear for music, displayed on untimely occasions. The book mixes natural history, humor, and affection for a faithful friend.
26650-the-ducks-and-frogs-a-tale-of-the-:
Fanny Fire-Fly wrote this verse tale for children, published at Boston by Joseph H. Francis in 1849, with engravings by Hartwell from designs by Billings. It opens on a cheerful summer morning, when two ducks stroll to a brook, bathe, smooth their glossy feathers, and swim together. Loud tones of sad lament stop them, and beneath bushes among reeds they find a company of long-faced frogs.

A frog orator in bottle green addresses the meeting, explaining that the frogs have not come to break the peace or plot mischief. They seek a grave petition to the men who rule, asking pity for their sad condition and safety in their quiet bogs. Ducks and frogs join in a gentle animal fable about pleading for the weak before power.
26937-a-syllabus-of-kentucky-folk-songs:
Hubert G. Shearin, professor of English philology at Transylvania University, and Josiah H. Combs compiled this syllabus, printed at Lexington, Kentucky, in 1911 as Transylvania University Studies in English, number two. It is a syllabus, not a songbook: each entry names a Kentucky variant, gives its stanza pattern, and sums up its plot. The first group gathers survivors of English and Scottish originals found in the Child collection.

Entries run from the King's Daughter and Pretty Polly, variants on Lady Isabel and the Elf Knight. They continue through Fair Ellender of the Earl Brand cycle, Lord Randal, and Edward. They reach the Greenwood Side of the Cruel Mother, Lord Bateman of Young Beichan, Barbara Allen, and the House Carpenter of the Demon Lover. Later groups turn to Kentucky's own murders and legends, from the Irish peddler shot from ambush to John Hardy's execution on the Tug River.
27530-the-tailor-and-the-crow-an-old-rhy:
L. Leslie Brooke gave this old rhyme new drawings in a picture book published by Frederick Warne in London and New York, with a 1911 copyright entered at Stationers' Hall. Brooke dedicates the book to his wife, and the rhyme itself begins with a carrion crow sat.

Brooke's children's books, listed in the volume, include Oranges and Lemons, The Man in the Moon, Little Bo-Peep, and This Little Pig Went to Market. The Tailor and the Crow belongs with those nursery favorites. Young readers get a short, funny rhyme, brightly pictured for reading aloud.
27678-nine-little-goslings:
Susan Coolidge's 1875 book retells nine nursery tales and rhymes, including Curly Locks, Goosey Goosey Gander, Little Bo-Peep, Mistress Mary, and Lady Bird. Published by Roberts Brothers of Boston with illustrations, it followed her popular Katy books.

Coolidge frames the old rhymes with verses about Mother Goose herself, imagined rocking at a child's cradle. The collection was meant for reading aloud at bedtime, giving familiar rhymes a gentle narrative setting for young children. The Boston printing lists nine rhymes on its title page, from Curly Locks to Up, Up, Up, and Down, Down, Down-y.
2777-cabbages-and-kings:
O. Henry wrote this novel of a banana republic, quoting the Walrus on talking of shoes and ships and sealing wax, and cabbages and kings. The little saint with a color more lightful than orange opens a tale of revolution, exiles, and American adventurers.

Anchuria, a fictional Central American port, fills with presidents, consuls, and fugitives, all chasing fortune or escape. O. Henry writes with wit and irony, linking short stories into a loose, sparkling whole. The book coined the banana republic, and it remains his most ambitious comic invention.
28109-how-to-make-rugs:
Candace Wheeler's How to Make Rugs, published in 1902 with a 1908 reissue, is a practical manual for home rug making. Wheeler, author of Principles of Home Decoration, argues that America lacked home industries that could earn families money. Rugs, woven at home from rags and wool, could fill that gap.

Chapters cover looms, patterns, dyeing, and the making of ingrain, woollen, cotton, and linsey-woolsey rugs, with notes on neighbourhood workshops. Pictures show looms, borders, and finished rugs by name. The book remains useful for craft readers and for historians of women's work at home.
28569-makers-of-many-things:
Eva March Tappan's Makers of Many Things, book 3 of the Industrial Readers, was published by Houghton Mifflin in 1916. Tappan opens with a dead fire, a failed last match, and no flint or steel, ten miles from a store. A trudge through snow to a neighbor teaches respect for the men who invented and perfected the little friction match.

Chapters then explain India rubber, kid gloves, paper from rags and trees, bookmaking, pens and pencils, dishes, watch wheels, shoes, cotton mills, and silkworms. Early matches dipped in sulphuric acid cost five dollars a hundred, and later sandpaper matches sold eighty-four for twenty-five cents. Readers get everyday objects explained by their making.
2867-a-sappho-of-green-springs:
Bret Harte's A Sappho of Green Springs collects four California stories, opening with the title tale in the editorial room of the Excelsior Magazine. An uncertain visitor hesitates at the door while the editor, pencil in mouth and proof slip in hand, stares at the intruder. The volume adds The Chatelaine of Burnt Ridge, Through the Santa Clara Wheat, and A Maecenas of the Pacific Slope.

Harte's later California work favors capable women, including a businesswoman whom men respect and admire rather than pursue for her fortune. The stories balance mining-camp humor with quieter scenes of work and independence. Together they show Harte moving beyond his early gold-rush sketches toward character studies of the settled West.
29020-a-boy-i-knew-and-four-dogs:
Laurence Hutton wrote this 1898 memoir, A Boy I Knew and Four Dogs, published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London, profusely illustrated. The book's front matter lists Hutton's other works, from Literary Landmarks of Rome, Florence, Venice, Jerusalem, London, and Edinburgh to Portraits in Plaster and Curiosities of the American Stage. A picture of Thackeray and the boy fronts the memoir.

Hutton recalls a boyhood shared with four dogs, in the warm, anecdotal style of his literary landmarks books. The memoir suits readers who like Victorian literary life told personally, with dogs as companions and authors as friends. Readers get a gentle, illustrated recollection, more about character and affection than about events, from a well-known American man of letters.
30647-mystery-at-geneva-an-improbable-ta:
Rose Macaulay writes Mystery at Geneva, an improbable tale of singular happenings, published in London, Glasgow, Melbourne, and Auckland in 1922 by W. Collins Sons. Macaulay, author of Dangerous Ages and Potterism, opens with a Greek phrase transliterated between plus marks in this text.

Transcriber notes record efforts to match the original closely, including spelling and hyphenation quirks, with lists of changes at the end. Macaulay sets a mystery among League-era Geneva figures, where singular happenings pile up into an improbable yet witty plot. The novel blends satire, suspense, and social comedy in a distinctly Macaulay voice.
31183-rembrandt-with-a-complete-list-of-:
Arthur M. Hind's 1912 volume, published by Frederick A. Stokes, pairs a short study of Rembrandt with a complete chronological list of his etchings. Illustrations range from an unfinished portrait of the artist's mother in 1628 and beggar scenes of 1630 through portraits of Saskia and the blind fiddler. They also show the return of the prodigal son and views of Amsterdam and the windmill.

Each entry carries its Bartsch number and notes on state, letting collectors trace how a plate changed across printings. For print lovers, the book is both an introduction to Rembrandt's etched work and a working checklist, compact enough to carry into a sale room or a museum print cabinet.
3128-saunterings:
Warner invites the reader to saunter with him, and warns at once against expecting instruction. Almost everyone has been somewhere and written about it, he jokes, so the only honest compromise is to go somewhere and learn nothing about it. The public's dislike of information in a book of this kind is, he says, perfectly justifiable, and the volume is poorly fitted to serve as a school text.

That teasing preface sets the terms for a set of idle travel pieces: talk, scenery, and passing talk, with no lessons forced on the reader. The pleasure is in the pace itself, a stroll rather than a march, where a writer's company matters more than his facts and the road is taken for its own sake.
31390-the-may-flower-and-miscellaneous-w:
Harriet Beecher Stowe's May Flower and Miscellaneous Writings, published by Phillips, Sampson in Boston in 1855, collects New England sketches first issued under that title. The introduction quotes G. B. Emerson on the mayflower itself. He calls it fragrant pearly-white or rose flowers rising from beneath a snow bank, the earliest harbinger of spring, abundant about Plymouth. It was the first flower to salute the Mayflower's storm-beaten crew after their first terrible winter.

Stowe makes the flower an emblem of Puritan faith, hope, and piety, a product of the hardest rocky soils drawing beauty from air more than earth. She notes the original series had limited circulation and was now out of print. The volume preserves her early sketches alongside miscellaneous writings, showing the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin in her New England vein.
32189-the-raising-and-care-of-guinea-pig:
A. C. Smith's The Raising and Care of Guinea Pigs was published by the author in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1915. It is a complete guide to breeding, feeding, housing, exhibiting, and marketing cavies. Its ten chapters run from Introduction and Varieties through Uses of Guinea Pigs and Food and Feeding. They continue to Housing, Breeding, Exhibiting, and Selling and Shipping. Diseases and Profits in Cavy Raising close the book.

The introduction calls the guinea pig or cavy a member of the rabbit family and a native of South America. It wonders why they are called guinea pigs, unless their shape suggests a small pig and Guinea may corrupt Guiana, a South American country. Readers get a practical cavy-keeper's manual, written when guinea pigs were farm stock as much as pets, with profits in view alongside feeding and housing.
32191-the-sentimental-vikings:
R. V. Risley's The Sentimental Vikings, published by John Lane at the Bodley Head in New York and London in 1897 and dedicated to E. F. C., gathers six tales of the old North. Its contents run from The Sweeping of the Hall and An Incident through Where the Wolves Dance and The Sacrilege to The Story of the Oar-Captain and The Last Voyage. The first tale is a Danish tragedy, told by Witlaf the harper in the hall of Gorm, king of Denmark, long ago.

Witlaf waves his handless arms in the firelight as he tells of Snore, lord of Zeeland's northern part, who swept his hall as day broke. At Snore's birth, men say, the heavens darkened, storm clouds swept low over the battlements, and voices sounded in the air. Readers get sentimental Viking tales. Harpers, kings, wolves, and sacrilege fill them, told by firelight.
32261-a-frenchman-in-america-recollectio:
Max O'Rell's A Frenchman in America was published in New York by Cassell in 1891, with over a hundred and thirty illustrations by E. W. Kemble. It records a Frenchman's recollections of men and things in the United States. O'Rell, author of Jonathan and His Continent, John Bull, Junior, and Jacques Bonhomme, writes as a lecturer and traveller, amused and observant by turns.

His chapters run from Departure, the Atlantic, and the demoralization of the boarders, with betting, an auctioneer, and an inquisitive Yankee. They continue through arrival, the custom house, and first looks at American newspapers, to impressions of American hotels. Later chapters treat his opening lecture, audiences he has had, the man who will not smile, and the one who laughs too soon. Readers get a humorous French view of America, from lecture halls to hotels.
3232-songs-of-the-ridings:
F W Moorman dedicates these songs to the Yorkshire members of the Workers' Educational Association. The contents run from a dalesman's litany and Cambodunum to telling the bees and the two lamplighters. Our beck, Lord George, Jenny Storm, and the new Englishman follow, with the bells of Kirkby Overblow and the gardener and the robin.

Moorman writes the Ridings in their own voice, with dialect, dales, and working life at the center. The hungry forties, the flowers of Knaresborough Forest, and the miller by the shore ground the songs in place and hardship. The book preserves Yorkshire speech and song at a moment when both were changing, and it still sings best read aloud.
32372-dickens-s-children-ten-drawings:
Jessie Willcox Smith's picture book, copyrighted in 1912, gathers ten drawings of children from the novels of Charles Dickens. The subjects include Tiny Tim with Bob Cratchit on Christmas Day, David Copperfield beside Peggotty by the parlour fire, and Paul Dombey and Florence on the beach at Brighton. Little Nell also appears with her grandfather at Mrs. Jarley's.

Pip and Joe Gargery, Jenny Wren the dolls' dressmaker, and Oliver meeting the Artful Dodger also appear. Later plates show Mrs. Kenwigs with her four small children, the runaway couple from the Christmas stories, and Little Em'ly from David Copperfield. Each drawing pairs a single scene with its novel and chapter, so readers can place the moment in the story. Smith's warm, clear style makes the volume a gentle introduction to Dickens for younger readers and a keepsake for older ones.
32504-all-about-the-three-little-pigs:
All About the Three Little Pigs, pictured by Dick Hartley and L. Kirby-Parrish and published in New York by Cupples and Leon, retells the classic tale for very young children. The volume belongs to the All About series, priced at thirty-five cents. Its companions include All About Peter Rabbit, All About the Three Bears, All About Mother Goose, and All About Cinderella, each pictured for small readers.

Three pigs build houses, meet a wolf, and learn that haste and laziness cost dearly, while solid work and a strong house save the day. Hartley and Kirby-Parrish's pictures carry much of the story, making it easy for parents to read aloud and for children to follow. The book suits bedtime reading and first encounters with a beloved nursery tale.
32788-more-conjuring-simple-tricks-for-s:
Hercat offers simple tricks for social gatherings, published in London by Dean and Son in 1912. The author of Hercat's Card Tricks and Conjuring Up to Date writes for amateurs who want effects that can be repeated without fear of detection.

Card tricks find a selected card at any number requested, shake one through a handkerchief, and discover one in a lighted cigarette. Coin tricks make a shilling penetrative, vanish a coin from cheek to elbow, and obey a sixpence. Handkerchief, ring, and candle tricks follow, with arithmetical problems that name a number thought of or erased, tell a lady's age, and predict the hour a friend intends to rise.
33992-autobiography-of-z-s-hastings:
Z. S. Hastings wrote this autobiography for his boys Harry, Paul, Otho, and Milo, dated at Effingham, Kansas, at Christmas 1911. Hastings was born on March 15, 1838, at Williams, in Lawrence County, Indiana, as the place is now called. His mother thought he looked like her brother Zachariah, his father like his brother Simpson, so he was named Zachariah Simpson.

Chapters cover birth, name, parents' religion, blood, ancestors' religion and politics, and a family move from North Carolina to Indiana. Hastings writes in a plain, homely voice for his children and theirs. The book preserves one Indiana family's story in its own words.
3465-under-two-flags:
Ouida, the pen name of Maria Louise Rame, writes a military romance about a young Englishman who flees disgrace at home. He enlists under a false name in the French Foreign Legion in Algeria. The story was first written for a military magazine, and soldiers praised its detail. Its hero serves under two flags in spirit: the England he left and the France whose uniform he wears.

The novel follows desert marches, comradeship, duels, and a love that crosses rank and nation. Ouida writes with high color and strong feeling, and the book became one of her most popular works. Readers who enjoy romantic adventure with a soldier hero will find passion, honor, and a vivid picture of colonial North Africa.
3636-the-fall-of-the-nibelungs:
Margaret Armour translates the German epic of the Nibelungs in this volume, called The Fall of the Nibelungs. The story is told in adventures, from Siegfried's youth and his coming to Worms, through his fight with the Saxons, his first sight of Kriemhild, and Gunther's wooing of Brunhild in Iceland. Later adventures follow Siegfried's journey to the Nibelung land and his return to Worms.

The second half turns to betrayal, murder, and revenge, as Kriemhild's grief drives kings and heroes to a hall of slaughter. Dankwart fights in the hall, brings news to his masters, and watches the dead thrown down. The book suits readers who want the great German legend in English, in its old episodic form.
4027-little-songs:
A book of little songs for little boys and girls aims to catch the good-humored nonsense that makes Mother Goose dear to children. The preface, dated Cambridge 1832, hopes children will lisp the rhymes while parents find no fault in them.

Songs about the moon, the whip, and nursery playthings fill the pages in short, musical lines. Look at the moon, the verses urge, shining like a lamp in the air and lighting the nursery floor. The book suits very young readers and adults reading aloud, offering simple rhymes for bedtime and play.
4215-oak-openings:
James Fenimore Cooper's Oak Openings, set among the oak openings of Michigan, follows a bee-hunter watching Indian canoes by moonlight. A bright moon reflects the sun's light for about an hour after sunset, and by its aid the hunter, still in his tree, watches canoes move.

Their people soon grow indistinct, and verse from Freneau warns that timorous fancy will long see painted chiefs and pointed spears. Cooper mixes frontier adventure with romance and moral reflection. Readers who enjoy Cooper's wilderness tales will find a late, thoughtful novel of the borderland.
441-new-poems-and-variant-readings:
Robert Louis Stevenson left these poems scattered among collectors, and Lloyd Osbourne gathered them in this 1918 volume. Love poems, songs, and short lyrics fill the pages, many withheld by Stevenson in life for their frank, personal tone. Variant readings show how he shaped lines across drafts.

Pieces range from prayers and spring songs to verses on Antony and Cleopatra and the northern lights. Osbourne notes their sincere, uneven charm, and the care with which Stevenson kept them through years of travel. The book gives readers a closer, more private Stevenson than his famous tales allow.
442-love-songs:
Sara Teasdale gathers love lyrics, old and new, in this 1917 volume, later reprinted in 1918. Beside fresh poems stand lyrics drawn from Rivers to the Sea and Helen of Troy, some lightly revised. Sections move from barter and twilight to songs out of sorrow and later, quieter love.

Teasdale writes in short, clear lines, with images of sea, night, and spring. Love here is tender, brief, and often lost, yet never bitter. The book won wide praise for its plain music, and it remains a gentle entry to Teasdale's art: feeling said simply, and said well.
4510-watersprings:
Arthur Christopher Benson published Watersprings in 1913, opening in bright February sunlight in the court of Beaufort College, Cambridge. The novel follows a young Cambridge man through college life, country visits, and family ties, with chapters on restlessness, the home circle, the vicar, and a country house called Windlow. Maud, Jack, and Howard are among the people who shape his choices.

As the story moves between Cambridge and the country, courtship, friendship, and questions of duty and belief come to the fore, leading to a wedding, a child, and a new life. Benson writes in a quiet, reflective manner, paying close attention to place and mood. Readers get a gentle Edwardian novel about growing up, settling down, and learning what love and work should mean.
5272-the-sea-fogs:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Sea Fogs, introduced by Thomas Rutherford Bacon, turns on the mists that beset much of the California coast. Bacon's introduction recalls Stevenson's arrival in California in 1879 to marry, his broken health. Stevenson called the sea fogs poisonous to a man with weak lungs, yet bracing and glorious to others.

The volume follows Stevenson through illness, marriage in May 1880. A honeymoon follows, spent squatting at Silverado on Mount Saint Helena, above the Napa Valley. Readers get a short, affectionate portrait of the writer's courage and determination to be happy, set against the fog-bound coast that shaped his California years.
5723-press-cuttings:
Bernard Shaw's Press Cuttings, dated 1913, is a short play set in the War Office on the morning of the first of April, 1911. General Mitchener sits at his writing table opening letters, while the machinery of government, press, and public opinion gathers around him. Shaw turns official business into comedy, letting generals, clerks, and journalists expose the gap between orders and sense.

The play's bite comes from its timing and talk: serious men handle absurd situations with perfect gravity, and Shaw lets their own words undo them. Readers and theatre groups will find a compact Shaw satire, easy to stage and sharp to quote. It suits those who enjoy political comedy that treats war offices and newspapers as twin stages for human folly.
6337-the-boy-allies-under-two-flags:
Boom, boom, speak the forward guns of the little scout cruiser H.M.S. Sylph, under Lord Hastings, as Jack in the pilot house cries a hit and Frank shouts good work to gunners who cannot hear him. A broadside follows, then German cruisers Breslau and Goeben answer from more than a mile away, shells throwing water in geysers round the little vessel like a typhoon. None finds its mark as the ships draw closer.

Ensign Robert L. Drake's Boy Allies tale follows Jack and Frank under two flags through Mediterranean fighting, with marksmanship as a test of nerve. Frank, challenged, fires twice at a knot on a tree, splintering it in midair with the second bullet, and tells a staggered midshipman he could have killed him with ease. The book is boys' war adventure, brisk, patriotic, and fond of guns, ships, and cool heads.
6429-many-ways-for-cooking-eggs:
Mrs. S. T. Rorer, author of Philadelphia cook books and Bread and Bread Making, gives many ways for cooking eggs, with sauces first. English drawn butter, plain hollandaise, anchovy, bechamel, tarragon, horseradish, cream, brown butter, Perigueux, tomato, paprika, curry, and Italian sauces open the book. Cooking of eggs follows, from preserving and egging and crumbing to shirred eggs, Mexicana, and eggs on a plate.

De Lesseps, Meyerbeer, a la Reine, au miroir, a la paysanne, and a la Trinidad join Rossini, baked in tomato sauce, and a la Suisse with nut brown butter. Birds' nests separate eggs, beat whites to stiff froth, heap them in dishes, make a hole, and drop in a whole yolk, then stand the dish in water and cover. Rorer writes a cook's catalogue, practical and generous, where one plain food becomes a hundred dishes.
6459-the-girl-aviators-on-golden-wings:
Margaret Burnham's second Girl Aviators book opens on the great Nevada desert, white and glittering, dotted with gloomy clumps of sage brush. Peggy Prescott wrinkles her nose disdainfully at the view from the car window, and her brother Roy asks what she thinks of it. She will wait a while before answering, she says judicially, and Roy calls on Jimsy Bancroft, a lad his own age, with a slender, graceful girl beside him.

Jimsy laughs that there is plenty of desert anyhow, much like what he expected, and Peggy feels like a regular cowgirl already. A mid passage introduces an experienced plainsman who suggests lightening and adjusting their equipment, his odd manner of talking coming only at intervals. Peggy wonders if he acts a part, then doubts it as his gestures convince her otherwise. Burnham writes girls' flying adventure with desert, machines, and pluck.
6619-poems-and-songs:
Björnstjerne Björnson, the Norwegian poet, appears here in English verse kept in his own meters by Arthur Hubbell Palmer of Yale. Palmer's introduction notes a strange fact: a life of seventy-seven years yielded just two hundred pages of lyric verse, more than half written in about a dozen years. Yet what is true and strong, he says, finds room to grow without ink's aid.

The poems themselves mix thought, ire, and mirth, with a love of loud life's battles and a bard's pride in his nation. Palmer keeps the meters true, so the English sings like the Norwegian. Poems and Songs is a fine, short gateway to a Nobel poet's lyric heart.
7391-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Songs in Many Keys covers Holmes's middle years, 1849 to 1861, when he was lecturing, doctoring, and writing for every Boston occasion. The contents run from The Ploughman and Spring to songs after lectures on Wordsworth, Moore, Keats, and Shelley, and on to The Hudson and an ode for Washington's birthday. A farewell to James Russell Lowell and a Burns Club poem show his circle of friends.

The title fits: Holmes tries many keys here, from farmyard humor to civic ceremony. Beneath the occasional verse, the shadow of the coming Civil War gathers in poems about freedom and the Union. The volume is best read as a Boston poet's diary in verse, recording a dozen years of lectures, friendships, and public causes.
7394-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
War dominates this volume, which gathers Holmes's songs of 1862 to 1874. Army Hymn, God Save the Flag, a hymn after the Emancipation Proclamation, and a puritan war song called To Canaan show a Boston poet rallying the Union cause. The Ballad of the Boston Tea-Party looks back to an earlier rebellion, while Dorothy Q, a family portrait, gives the war years a quiet, domestic counterpoint.

After the fighting come songs of welcome and farewell, union and liberty, and the flower of liberty itself. Holmes wrote many of these for public occasions, and they carry the plain, singable patriotism that made him a civic poet. The volume stands as a verse record of how the Civil War sounded in Boston parlors and meeting halls.
7982-a-traveller-in-little-things:
W. H. Hudson gathered these sketches from the New Statesman, the Saturday Review, the Nation, and the Cornhill Magazine into a book of small observations. Its contents wander from a Surrey village and a Wiltshire village to apple blossoms and a lost village. The vanishing curtsey, little girls he had met, Cromer beach, wild flowers, and a dog named Dandy. Fourteen of the pieces had already appeared in magazines.

Hudson's gift is attention: he finds a whole story in a gesture, a lane, or a childhood memory. The sketches read like walks taken slowly, with pauses for birds, people, and old customs. For readers who love English nature writing, the book is a gentle classic, and a reminder that the smallest things can hold a traveller longest.
7998-the-frogs:
Aristophanes, the great Athenian comic playwright, wrote The Frogs in the late fifth century BC, and it appears here in the Harvard Classics volume of nine Greek dramas. The play sends Dionysus, god of theatre, down to the underworld to bring back a great tragedian, since Athens has lost its best poets. There he judges a contest between Aeschylus and Euripides, with the fate of the city's art, and its spirit, at stake.

The comedy is bawdy, musical, and brilliantly parodic, mocking both poets while celebrating what theatre can do. Its chorus of frogs gives the play its name and its most famous joke. For readers new to Greek comedy, it is the friendliest starting point: funny on the surface, serious underneath, and still performed today.
8011-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
First Kings opens with David's death and Solomon's rise, then follows the building of the temple in Jerusalem, the king's wisdom and wealth, and his later drift into idolatry. After Solomon, the kingdom splits: Rehoboam keeps Judah, Jeroboam takes Israel, and a parade of kings follows, most of them faithless. Into this decline steps Elijah, whose contest with the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel is the book's dramatic centre.

The history is told as moral account, with each king judged by faithfulness. Solomon's glory and Elijah's fire give the book its two poles: splendour and prophecy. In the King James Version, the temple building, the Queen of Sheba's visit, and Elijah's miracles remain among the Old Testament's most vivid passages.
8012-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
From Solomon's successors to the fall of Jerusalem, the second book of Kings tells the story of a divided kingdom. Israel in the north and Judah in the south drift toward idolatry and foreign alliances, warned by prophets Elijah and Elisha, whose miracles and confrontations fill the middle chapters. One kingdom after another falls: Israel to Assyria, and Judah, after a last reform under Josiah, to Babylon and exile.

The book reads as both history and judgment, explaining disaster as the fruit of unfaithfulness. Its vivid episodes, from Elijah on Carmel to the siege of Jerusalem, have entered common language. In the King James Version, the narrative's steady, sombre pace suits its theme: a people who had been given a land, losing it through their kings' choices.
8184-the-ghost-kings:
H. Rider Haggard's novel The Ghost Kings follows Rachel and Noie through a Zulu world of kings, omens, and spirits. Its chapters move from a girl and a boy, through goodbye and Ishmael, the casting of lots and the message of the king. To the taking of Noie, the omen of a star, a visit to the Inkosazana, Rachel's vision, and her loss and recovery of her spirit. Later chapters reach the mother of the trees, the city of the dead, the sanctuary, and a dream in the north.

Haggard writes adventure steeped in African legend, with Rachel as a white girl caught between two worlds and their spiritual powers. The novel's supernatural machinery, visions, curses, and ghost kings, drives its romance. For Haggard readers, it is a characteristic late romance, rich in atmosphere and in the author's fascination with Zulu belief.
8238-the-world-english-bible-web-1-kings:
First Kings, in the World English Bible, opens with David old and stricken in years, kept warm by the young Abishag the Shunammite, while Adonijah exalts himself, saying he will be king. The book, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, follows Solomon's rise, the temple's building, his wisdom and later idolatry, the kingdom's split, and Elijah's stand against Baal. Its modern prose keeps the court intrigues vivid.

Readers meet a history told as moral account, where kings are judged by faithfulness. The World English Bible's plain style suits the narrative's pace, from palace plots to Carmel's fire. For those approaching Kings for the first time, this version offers the story without archaic language getting in the way.
8239-the-world-english-bible-web-2-kings:
Second Kings, in the World English Bible, opens with Moab rebelling after Ahab's death, and Ahaziah falling through a lattice in his upper chamber at Samaria. Sick, he sends messengers to inquire of Baal Zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. But Yahweh's angel tells Elijah to meet them and ask why Israel seeks a god of Ekron when there is a God in Israel. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book follows Elijah and Elisha, the divided kingdoms, and exile.

The modern version keeps the prophets' miracles and the kings' failures vivid, from chariots of fire to the fall of Jerusalem. Second Kings here reads as a sombre history of a divided people losing its land. For readers of the histories, this rendering gives the story plainly, with its judgments intact.
8865-miss-theodosia-s-heartstrings:
Annie Hamilton Donnell writes Miss Theodosia's Heartstrings, illustrated by William Van Dresser, and dedicates it. A smile, to her husband, who could write so much better a book and dedicate it to her. Illustrations promise delicate fingers undoing the ravages of Stefana's patient endeavours, beautiful names except poor Elly, a girl asking to be put into a story like that. Evangeline establishing a stage of action outside the window. Chapter one opens with an exclamation: mercy gracious, answered by Miss Theodosia Baxter herself, a woman of few words.

The novel follows Theodosia, a New England spinster of strong feelings and stronger principles, through household, church. Neighbourhood life, where heartstrings are tugged by children, neighbours, and old romances. Donnell writes gently and humorously about a woman society might overlook.
9093-rural-tales-ballads-and-songs:
Robert Bloomfield published these rural tales, ballads, and songs in London in 1802, in the gap between The Farmer's Boy and its sequel. Written while his fame was fresh, the pieces treat village manners and country scenes, from a widow and her hour-glass to the Fakenham Ghost and the love of Walter and Jane. Bloomfield offers them on their moral merit.

The verse is plain, kind, and rooted in farm work, seasons, and parish life. Bloomfield, a working man himself, wrote from inside that world, not above it. The book keeps its charm as a record of English country life at the turn of the century, told in song.
9548-honore-de-balzac-his-life-and-writi:
Mary F. Sandars wrote Honoré de Balzac: His Life and Writings, first published in 1904, a life of the great French novelist. Sandars notes that little true life writing on Balzac then existed in English, though his fame stood high. Her book traces his complex mind, his debts, his toil, and his vast human comedy. She claims Balzac first gave plain men and women full weight in fiction.

Chapters follow Balzac from youth to fame, showing how he found drama in daily life, not in wild plots. His creed, drawn from Burns, holds that a man is a man for all that, rich or poor. A reader gets a clear, warm life of a giant novelist, and a guide to why his crowded world still draws readers today.
9809-the-price-of-things:
Elinor Glyn wrote The Price of Things in 1919, a novel of love, thought, and honeymoon discontent. Amaryllis Ardayre, on honeymoon in Paris at the Russian Embassy, hears a Russian claim that happiness needs banished thought. She puzzles at his words, having lived in the country as good as gold. Her husband Sir John seems dull beside school friend Elsie's promised thrills.

Glyn follows Amaryllis from Paris parties to a reckoning with desire, will, and the cost of probing life's meaning. Pandora's box opens as she thinks. A reader gets a frank, romantic Glyn novel, where a young wife learns what happiness truly prices.
9902-the-middle-of-things:
J. S. Fletcher's 1922 mystery opens with a man faced with reality, and a house at number seven in the square. Who was Ashton, and what do a ring and a knife mean? The early chapters send the searcher looking for a missing man, weighing speculations and secrets.

Later clues lead to a parish register, a visit to Paris, a grey mare inn, and a Japanese cabinet, as the middle of things slowly untangles. Fletcher, a prolific writer of detective tales, keeps the plot turning on small, concrete clues. Mystery readers get a neat puzzle in the classic British manner.
a-sappho-of-green-springs:
Bret Harte gathers four California tales, opening with the title story in the office of the Excelsior Magazine. A tall, dust-covered stranger with a long beard hesitates at the editor's door, carrying verses by a young woman of Green Springs whose poems have startled the magazine's readers. Who she is, and who speaks for her, drives the tale.

The Chatelaine of Burnt Ridge, Through the Santa Clara Wheat, and A Maecenas of the Pacific Slope complete the volume. Harte writes of editors, ranch families, and wheat country with his usual blend of sentiment and dry comedy. The title story plays gently with literary fame in a mining state.
a-traveller-in-little-things: William Henry Hudson gathers a traveller's sketches of little things in this volume. Fourteen first appeared in the New Statesman, the Saturday Review, the Nation, and the Cornhill Magazine. The contents run from how he found his title and an old man's delusion through stories of two brothers. Two white houses, a dog named Dandy, and a samphire gatherer follow. Surrey and Wiltshire villages, apple blossoms, freckles, Cromer beach, and a jackdaw complete the gathering.
anne-severn-and-the-fieldings: May Sinclair writes Anne Severn and the Fieldings, opening with children and following its heroine through the Fielding family world. The novel traces love, duty, and self-knowledge across years, in Sinclair's psychologically alert prose. It stands among her best studies of women's lives in early twentieth-century England. The close ties feeling to choice with care.
cabbages-and-kings:
O. Henry set this book of linked stories in Coralio, a port in the fictional republic of Anchuria on the Caribbean coast of Central America. The title comes from the Walrus and the Carpenter verses quoted at the front. A proem by the carpenter frames the tales, and the first story, Fox-in-the-Morning, starts the flight of a president.

President Miraflores flees his capital with the treasury funds and a singer, and the American adventurers of Coralio close in. Frank Goodwin, the banana magnate, and Billy Keogh, the cheerful photographer, run through the episodes. Lotus eating, forged telegrams, a suicide, and a hidden fortune braid the stories together. O. Henry wrote the book out of his own months in Honduras, and the banana republic he invented here entered the language.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-barl:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Barlings describes a Norbertine abbey about six miles east-north-east of Lincoln, founded in 1154 by Ralph de Haye and dedicated to Our Lady. Ralph gave lands to the Abbot of Newhouse, England's first Norbertine house, asking for a colony of White Canons at Barlings.

The abbey later moved to Oxeney in the same township, where Henry the Eighth dissolved it in 1537. Bishop Redman's register of visitations supplies much of what is known about Barlings and other English Norbertine houses. The register, kept in the Bodleian Library, covers some thirty-five years of visits and was published as Collectanea Anglo-Premonstratensia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthon-rafael:
Anton Raphael Mengs, Bohemian painter, born 1728, died 1779. He learned from his father Ismael, who moved to Rome in 1741. From his youth Mengs was energetic and skilful, appointed court painter before sixteen. He declined with modesty, returning to Rome to study.

He painted the Parnassus at the Villa Albani. He then went to Naples, executing a Caserta altar-piece, but quickly returned to Rome, then pressed into Charles III's service. He arrived at Madrid in 1761. Here he carried out many commissions, becoming St. Ferdinand Academy director. Once more he went back to Rome for his health. He returned to Madrid in 1773, painting the Apotheosis of Trajan for Charles III. Again his health broke down, and he returned to Rome. He died there, buried in San Michele church. His pastel and crayon works are among his finest. Many paintings are in Dresden and Vienna, with miniature portraits and Raphael copies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-konin:
Anthony Konings, born Helmond 1821, died 1884. After a brilliant humanities course he entered the seminary, conspicuous for piety. Feeling a monastic call, he entered the novitiate in 1842. His superiors sent him to higher studies. After teaching humanities, he was called onward.

His Moral Theology, Boston, 1874, based on Gury, won approval for simple language and succinct Alphonsus form. He first expounded the saint's views on equiprobabilism methodically. His American law knowledge enhanced his work's value. Later, at Bishop Mullen's suggestion, he published on episcopal faculties, revised and enlarged by Putzer. His pamphlet De Absolutione Parentibus was taken by the Holy Office as the basis of an Instruction to American bishops. Its very words entered the Third Baltimore Council Acts. Since then this Instruction has been the norm for absolving such parents. Konings was consulted across the United States, examined candidates, and served as an expert in ecclesiastical trials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chronology-of:
An entry on the chronology of the kings of Judah and Israel, built first on a table of Bible data. For Judah the table gives each king, his age, length of reign, year of accession, and Bible reference, with s for son and b for brother of his predecessor. For Israel it gives length of reign, accession year, and reference, from Jeroboam the First through Hoshea.

The tables run from David, aged thirty with a forty-year reign, and Solomon through Asa and Josaphat. Israel's side runs from Nadab and Baasha through Ahab, Jehu, and Jeroboam the Second. The entry then weighs the figures against each other and against outside history, sorting reigns, co-regencies, and rival counts. It is a working tool for readers tracing the divided monarchy year by year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical buildings cover every structure raised for liturgical acts, whether called church, chapel, oratory, or basilica. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats the subject under history, division, erection, repair, consecration, immunity, and fabric. In the earliest days no buildings were set apart for Eucharistic worship, and assemblies met in private houses, as Acts and the epistles show.

Gatherings in the Temple, synagogues, or hired halls served teaching or prayer, not the Eucharist. By the end of the second century, dedicated buildings appear, and the entry follows their growth, upkeep, and legal standing. It closes with wardens, their election, and their duty to priest and bishop, plus the state law of church property in English-speaking lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-and-jo:
Edmund and John Jennings were brothers from Lichfield who both turned Catholic in hard times. Edmund, born in 1567, trained at Reims, was ordained in 1590, and came back to England under a false name. Seized while saying Mass in London in November 1591, he was put to death at Gray's Inn Fields that December.

His death changed his younger brother John, who at first had rejoiced to be rid of his pleading. John later wrote Edmund's life, joined the Franciscans, and rebuilt the English province of the order, dying at Douai in 1660. The entry moves from a short, brave mission to a long life of repair, and it is a vivid window on Catholic England under Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jeremiah-will:
Jeremiah Williams Cummings, an American priest and publicist born at Washington in 1814 and dead in New York in 1866. He was sent by Bishop Dubois to Rome's Propaganda College after his father's death moved the family to New York. Winning his doctorate, he returned as assistant at Saint Patrick's Cathedral.

Cummings proved a linguist, writer, musician, and popular preacher, and in 1848 Bishop Hughes set him to found Saint Stephen's parish. Intimate friend and disciple of Orestes Brownson, he managed Brownson's lectures and wrote often for his Review, sometimes more bluntly than Brownson himself.
